--- title: "One call, end to end" --- A `Scenario` is a description of a place and a plan, where the place is fixed by the survey and the entomology and the plan is whatever changes at the campaign, and `run_scenarios` takes a list of those descriptions and returns a table. The two objects are plain dataclasses, importable from either `estimint` or `estimint.scenarios`. ```python from estimint import run_scenarios from estimint.scenarios import Scenario, EirTarget ``` ## The seven required fields These have no defaults and must be given for every scenario, and together they describe the setting as it stands, before anything is done to it. | Field | Meaning | |---|---| | `name` | A label. It is echoed into the results and is how you index them afterwards. | | `res_use` | Pyrethroid resistance, 0 (fully susceptible) to 1 (fully resistant). | | `Q0` | Human blood index, 0 to 1. | | `phi` | Share of bites taken while people are in bed. Enters the emulator as `phi_bednets`. | | `seasonal` | 0 for perennial transmission, 1 for strongly seasonal. | | `irs` | IRS coverage currently in place. Enters the emulator as `irs_use`. | | `eir_target` | An `EirTarget`. How transmission intensity is specified. | Three of these are renamed on the way in, so that `phi` becomes `phi_bednets` and `irs` becomes `irs_use`, while `res_use` is not a covariate at all, being consumed by the `dn0` curves and never reaching the emulator. What the emulator sees is the [twelve static covariates](../05-statemint/covariates.qmd). ## The three input modes `EirTarget(input_value, input_mode)` says what quantity you are handing over, and because the emulator only ever runs from an EIR, the mode decides how much work estiMINT does first. | Mode | You supply | What happens | |---|---|---| | `"prevalence"` | Under-5 parasite prevalence in [0.005, 0.80] | estiMINT inverts it to an EIR with the XGBoost prevalence model. | | `"eir"` | An EIR, infectious bites per person per year | Used directly. No inversion. | | `"hbr"` | A human biting rate | Converted to an EIR through the HBR model. | Use `"prevalence"` when the evidence is a cross-sectional survey, which is the case for the district worked through here; use `"eir"` when the EIR is already in hand, or is the quantity you are sweeping over; and use `"hbr"` when the evidence is entomological. `mosquito_delta` only applies to `"prevalence"`, so supplied alongside an `"eir"` or `"hbr"` input it is silently ignored, because there is no prevalence-to-EIR step for it to modify. The mechanism is set out in [Mosquito density and EIR](../04-estimint/mosquito-density.qmd). ## The ten defaulted fields Everything else defaults, and every default is zero or `None`. | Field | Default | Meaning | |---|---|---| | `py_only` | `0.0` | Current coverage of pyrethroid-only nets. | | `py_pbo` | `0.0` | Current coverage of pyrethroid-PBO nets. | | `py_pyrrole` | `0.0` | Current coverage of pyrethroid-pyrrole nets. | | `py_ppf` | `0.0` | Current coverage of pyrethroid-PPF nets. | | `mosquito_delta` | `0.0` | Proportional change in mosquito density. Must be > −1. | | `itn_future` | `0.0` | Net coverage from the campaign. | | `net_type_future` | `None` | Net product from the campaign. | | `irs_future` | `0.0` | IRS coverage from the campaign. | | `routine` | `0.0` | Routine (continuous) net distribution from the campaign. | | `lsm` | `0.0` | Larval source management coverage from the campaign. | The first four are the current net mix, whose coverages are summed to give `itn_use` and whose `dn0` values are averaged to give `dn0_use`, while the rest describe the campaign. `routine` and `lsm` carry no `_future` suffix but belong to the campaign all the same, and like `dn0_future`, `itn_future` and `irs_future` they are held at zero for every timestep before day 3285, taking their supplied value only from the campaign onwards. ::: {.callout-important} ## Future coverage must be set explicitly If `itn_future` is 0 or `net_type_future` is `None`, then `dn0_future` and `itn_future` are both set to 0, and the nets are **withdrawn** at the campaign. `irs_future` behaves the same way and does not inherit from `irs`. To hold an intervention steady you must restate it, so a district with pyrethroid-only nets at 0.70 that intends to keep them needs `itn_future=0.70, net_type_future="pyrethroid_only"` written out in full. If it is omitted, the district has been modelled as abandoning nets, and the rebound in the trajectory is real output from a scenario that was not intended. ::: ## One call The district has measured under-5 prevalence 0.45, pyrethroid resistance 0.30, pyrethroid-only nets at 0.70 coverage, perennial transmission and no IRS. The plan is to switch those nets to PBO at the same coverage. ::: {#e79f7776 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} from estimint import run_scenarios from estimint.scenarios import Scenario, EirTarget pbo = Scenario( name="PBO", res_use=0.30, Q0=0.85, phi=0.80, seasonal=0.0, irs=0.0, eir_target=EirTarget(0.45, "prevalence"), py_only=0.70, # the nets in place now itn_future=0.70, # the campaign net_type_future="pyrethroid_pbo", ) res = run_scenarios([pbo]) res.shape ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (1, 23) ``` ::: ::: The frame that comes back has one row and twenty-three columns. ::: {.callout-warning} ## Underscores, not hyphens `net_type_future` accepts `"pyrethroid_pbo"` or the short alias `"py_pbo"`, but it does not accept `"pyrethroid-pbo"`, and a hyphen raises `ValueError: unknown net type`. ::: ## What comes back The returned frame is one row per scenario, and its columns fall into four groups. The first group is **what you asked for, resolved**, giving the current net mix reduced to a single product name, together with the product used in the campaign. ::: {#e12883f5 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} res[["name", "input_mode", "net", "net_future"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
name input_mode net net_future
0 PBO prevalence py_only pyrethroid_pbo
``` ::: ::: With no campaign nets, `net_future` comes back as the string `"none"` rather than a missing value. The second group is **the covariates the emulator actually saw**, which are derived rather than echoed, so read them back to check that the scenario that ran is the one you built. ::: {#6e06d99b .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} res[[ "dn0_use", "itn_use", "irs_use", "dn0_future", "itn_future", "irs_future", "routine", "lsm", "seasonal", ]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
dn0_use itn_use irs_use dn0_future itn_future irs_future routine lsm seasonal
0 0.311 0.7 0.0 0.48495 0.7 0.0 0.0 0.0 0.0
``` ::: ::: `dn0_use` is the usage-weighted `dn0` of the current mix and `itn_use` the sum of its coverages, while `dn0_future` is the `dn0` of the campaign product at the same resistance. `lsm` is not always the `lsm` you passed, because `run_scenarios` folds PPF net coverage into effective larval source management before the emulator runs, under the rule set out in [Pipeline architecture](../07-under-the-hood/architecture.qmd). The third group is **transmission intensity**, where `eir_baseline` is what the inversion produced from the measured prevalence and `eir_final` is that EIR after `mosquito_delta` has been applied, which equals `eir_baseline` when the delta is zero. ::: {#97c023b2 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} res[["eir_baseline", "mosquito_delta", "eir_final", "hbr_baseline", "hbr_new"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
eir_baseline mosquito_delta eir_final hbr_baseline hbr_new
0 31.960129 0.0 31.960129 NaN NaN
``` ::: ::: `hbr_baseline` and `hbr_new` are `NaN` here, and will be for most scenarios. They are only populated when a prevalence input is combined with a non-zero `mosquito_delta`, because the HBR is an intermediate in that calculation and not otherwise computed. The fourth group is **outcomes**, where `prev_y9` is prevalence at the campaign and should be close to the 0.45 that was supplied, the small gap being the round trip through the inversion and the emulator. `prev_endline` and `cases_endline` are the last window of the horizon, three years later. ::: {#0ea8da1b .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} res[["prev_y9", "prev_endline", "cases_endline"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}
prev_y9 prev_endline cases_endline
0 0.456028 0.470118 2.412444
``` ::: ::: ## The trajectories The last two columns, `prevalence` and `cases`, are not scalars, and each cell holds the full trajectory as a 157-element NumPy array, stored inside the DataFrame rather than unrolled into a tidy long table. ::: {#25c54678 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np prev = np.asarray(res.loc[0, "prevalence"]) cases = np.asarray(res.loc[0, "cases"]) type(prev), prev.shape, prev.dtype ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` (numpy.ndarray, (157,), dtype('float32')) ``` ::: ::: This is convenient for a five-row grid and awkward for anything else. It means the frame cannot be written to CSV as it stands, and that any comparison across scenarios has to reach into the cells first. [Exporting results](exporting.qmd) deals with both. The 157 windows are a property of the emulator, so read the grid off the artefact rather than hard-coding it. `preload_models` returns the three estiMINT XGBoost models and the two stateMINT artefacts, which are the same objects `run_scenarios` uses internally, so calling it once up front also warms the caches and pulls the weights from HuggingFace before the first run rather than during it. ::: {#89bd1316 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} from estimint import preload_models xgb_models, artifacts = preload_models() cfg = artifacts["prevalence"].preprocessing_config n_steps = cfg["n_steps"] window = cfg["window_size"] start = cfg["model_start_day"] campaign = cfg["intervention_day"] abs_t = start + window * np.arange(n_steps) years = (abs_t - campaign) / 365 idx_y9 = int(np.argmin(np.abs(abs_t - campaign))) n_steps, window, start, campaign, idx_y9 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ``` (157, 14, 2190, 3285, 78) ``` ::: ::: `idx_y9` is the index of the window in which the campaign falls. Everything before it is baseline, everything from it onwards is response, and in `years` the campaign is at zero. ::: {#c63b2805 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} float(years[0]), float(years[idx_y9]), float(years[-1]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ``` (-3.0, -0.00821917808219178, 2.9835616438356163) ``` ::: ::: The horizon covers three years of baseline and three years of response. A trajectory can then be taken out of a cell and plotted against that axis in two lines. ::: {#e379979a .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots() ax.plot(years, prev, color="#00d4aa") ax.axvline(0, color="#8b93a3", ls="--", lw=1, alpha=0.7) ax.set_xlabel("Years since campaign") ax.set_ylabel("Prevalence (under 5)") ax.set_ylim(0, None) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Prevalence under the PBO campaign. The dashed line marks the campaign at year 0; everything to its left is the run-up under the nets already in place.](run-scenarios_files/figure-html/cell-11-output-1.png){fig-alt='Line chart of under-five prevalence from three years before the campaign to three years after. Before the campaign prevalence dips to about 0.29 and climbs back to about 0.46. After the campaign it falls to about 0.26 within a year, then rises again to about 0.47 by the end of the horizon.'} ::: ::: The three years to the left of the line are the model's run-up to the campaign under the nets already in place. The prevalence you supply is prevalence *at the campaign*, not at the start of the horizon, so the value to check against your input is `prev_y9` rather than the level anywhere in the run-up. After the campaign, prevalence reaches its minimum about a year in and rises again over the rest of the horizon. Whether it rebounds less far than the alternatives cannot be answered from one scenario. ## Pointing at other weights Both `run_scenarios` and `preload_models` take an `hf_repo` argument, defaulting to `"dide-ic/stateMINT"`. ```python res = run_scenarios([pbo], hf_repo="dide-ic/stateMINT") ``` Change it to run against a fork or a local snapshot of the weights. `run_scenarios` tracks whatever `main` currently points at in that repository and exposes no revision pin, so if an analysis has to be reproducible years from now, record the weight version alongside the results, or drive the emulator directly with a pinned `revision` as in [Calling the emulator](../05-statemint/the-emulator.qmd). ## Next - [A scenario grid](scenario-grid.qmd) — five campaigns, one baseline, one call. - [Covariates and the time grid](../05-statemint/covariates.qmd) — what the emulator sees. - [Nets and dn0](../04-estimint/nets-and-dn0.qmd) — where `dn0_use` and `dn0_future` come from.
